bio.en: Seth Godin is a marketer, teacher, entrepreneur, and author of more than 20 books, including Purple Cow, Permission Marketing, and Linchpin.
bio.zh: 赛斯·戈丁（Seth Godin）是营销思想家、教育者和创业者，著有《紫牛》《许可营销》《支点》等 20 余部作品，并通过长期写作持续影响人们对营销、品牌、产品与改变的理解。

summary.en: This episode explores how to build remarkable products that spread, create a strategy with productive tension, make a meaningful promise to users, and build brands that remain distinctive as AI becomes ubiquitous.
summary.zh: 本期围绕如何打造值得主动传播的产品、如何让策略保有有效张力、如何向用户作出并兑现一个有意义的承诺，以及当 AI 逐渐成为基础能力后，品牌怎样继续保持差异化展开。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before you came on, I asked on Twitter, what should I ask Seth Godin? The most recurring theme actually had to do with AI. How do you think all these new AI companies build brands to distinguish and differentiate themselves?
turns.zh: 在你上线之前，我在推特上问过：我该问赛斯·戈丁什么问题？最常被提及的主题其实是关于人工智能的。你如何看待所有这些新兴的AI公司如何打造品牌以突出自身特色？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: AI very soon is going to stop being a feature the same way electricity is not a feature. What AI companies and all companies need to do is say, what's in this for the user? What promise do I want to make a difficult promise, a remarkable promise, and then how do I keep it?
turns.zh: AI很快就不再是某种功能，就像电力不再是功能一样。AI公司和所有公司需要做的，就是思考：这对用户意味着什么？我们要许下什么样的承诺——一个艰难的承诺，一个非凡的承诺——然后如何兑现它？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You wrote a new book. You basically talk about how a great strategy has tension at the center of it.
turns.zh: 你写了一本新书。书中主要探讨了伟大战略的核心必定存在张力。

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Tension is at the heart of every art form and every innovation. What we do when we launch a new product, we say, we have this thing that can do X, and now the person is imagining what their life might be like if that were true. If they fall in love with that possibility, now there's tension. Did you tell the truth? Is it going to work for them?
turns.zh: 张力是每种艺术形式和每项创新的核心。当我们推出新产品时，我们会说：我们有这个能实现X的功能，现在用户开始想象如果这真的实现会是什么样子。如果他们爱上了这种可能性，就产生了张力。我们说实话了吗？它能为他们带来价值吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's the section that stuck out to me, these four insights that basically determine what your life is going to be like outside of actually building the product.
turns.zh: 书中有些章节让我印象深刻，这些四个洞察基本决定了你实际构建产品之外的生活会是什么样子。

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: For a product person, these are the critical choices and you probably have glossed over them.
turns.zh: 对于产品从业者来说，这些都是关键的选择，而你很可能忽视了它们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Today my guest is Seth Godin. Seth is an absolute legend. He's published 21 books, including 18 international bestsellers. He's been blogging every single day for almost 10,000 days in a row now. His writing and his advice have inspired me and so many people all over the world for the past few decades. He shares wisdom and advice around stuff that everyone can benefit from, including how ideas spread, when to quit, how to lead, how to stand out, and most of all how to change everything. In addition to his writing and speaking, Seth has founded several companies, including Yoyodyne and Squidoo. He also started the altMBA program, and as you'll hear in our conversation, he actually started his career as a product manager. In our conversation, Seth shares advice on how to know if you have good taste and how to build your taste, how to build a brand in an increasingly crowded world of AI startups and AI content, his thoughts on the Jaguar rebrand and also the Tesla Cybertruck. (02:10): We also delve into his new book, This is Strategy, including why every great strategy has tension at its center, why you need to understand the systems within which you operate in order to build a great strategy and how choosing your customers, your distribution strategy, and how you validate your idea will inform the product you build and the life that you live. We also talk about how he used Claude as a writing assistant in developing this new book. (02:33): This episode is short and packed with insights, which I know is what you all love. If you enjoy this podcast, don't forget to subscribe and follow it in your favorite podcasting app or YouTube. It's the best way to avoid missing future episodes and helps the podcast tremendously. With that, I bring you Seth Godin. (02:52): Seth, thank you so much for being here and welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 今天的嘉宾是赛斯·戈丁。赛斯绝对是个传奇人物。他出版了21本书，其中18本登上国际畅销书榜单。他几乎连续10,000天每天坚持写博客。过去几十年来，他的作品和建议激励着我和全世界无数人。他分享了每个人都能受益的智慧和建议，包括想法如何传播、何时退出、如何领导、如何脱颖而出，最重要的是如何改变一切。除了写作和演讲，赛斯还创立了多家公司，包括Yoyodyne和Squidoo。他还创办了altMBA项目，正如你将在我们的对话中听到的，他的职业生涯实际上始于产品经理。在我们的对话中，赛斯分享了如何判断你是否有好品味以及如何培养这种品味，如何在日益拥挤的AI初创公司和AI内容世界中建立品牌，他对捷豹品牌重塑和特斯拉Cybertruck的看法。（02:10）：我们还深入探讨了他的新书《这就是战略》，包括为什么每项伟大的战略都以张力为核心，为什么你需要理解自己所处的系统才能制定伟大的战略，以及如何选择客户、分销策略和验证你的想法将如何影响你构建的产品和你的生活。我们还谈到了他在开发这本新书时如何使用Claude作为写作助手。 （02:33）：本期节目简短而充满洞察力，我知道这正是你们所喜爱的。如果你们喜欢这个播客，别忘了在你们喜欢的播客应用或YouTube上订阅和关注。这是避免错过未来节目的最佳方式。说到这里，我为你们带来赛斯·戈丁。（02:52）：赛斯，非常感谢你能来参加节目，欢迎来到播客。

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: What a treat, Lenny. Thank you for having me. Lenny was my late mom's nickname, so it's good to say that out loud.
turns.zh: 真是太棒了，莱尼。感谢邀请我。莱尼是我已故母亲的昵称，所以能大声说出这个名字感觉很好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so cool. I've never heard it used for a woman, and every Lenny out there I've met is wonderful, so I imagine she's wonderful. First, I just want to say how honored I am to have you on this podcast. When I actually started this podcast, I was like, and I was listening to you on Tim Ferriss at that point, and I was like, man, what if one day I get Seth Godin on my podcast? How cool would that be? I've read so many of your books. I have a bunch of them in the bookshelf back there. I reference your stuff all the time, so thank you again for doing this.
turns.zh: 太酷了。我从没听过有人用这个称呼女性，而且我认识的莱尼们都很棒，所以我觉得她肯定很棒。首先，我想说很荣幸能邀请您做客我们的播客。刚开始做这个播客时，我当时正在听蒂姆·费里斯的节目，就想，如果哪天能邀请赛斯·高汀上我的节目，那该有多酷啊？我读过你很多书，书架上还摆着一堆。平时工作中也经常引用你的观点，再次感谢您接受这次采访。

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Well, thank you. It's a treat to talk to you.
turns.zh: 嗯，谢谢。能和您交流真是荣幸。

turns.zh: 今天的节目由DX赞助。如果您是工程团队的领导者，或者在平台团队工作，总有一天您的CEO会要求您提供生产力指标，但衡量工程团队的效率并不容易，我们都认同，像PR数量或提交次数这样的简单指标并不能完全反映全貌。这时候DX就能派上用场了。DX是由顶尖研究人员设计的工程智能解决方案，其中包括DORA和Space框架背后的团队。它将开发者工具的定量数据与开发者的定性反馈相结合，为您提供工程生产力及影响因素的全景视图。了解为什么Etsy、Dropbox、Twilio、Vercel和Webflow等全球知名公司都依赖DX。访问DX官网getdx.com/Lenny。（04:25）：本期节目由Vanta赞助。确保公司拥有一流的安全实践并不容易。现在，您可以通过单一平台Vanta评估风险、赢得客户信任，并实现SOC 2、ISO-27001、HIPAA等标准的合规。Vanta的市场领先信任管理平台帮助您持续监控合规情况，同时进行风险报告和追踪。此外，您还可以通过Vanta AI完成安全问卷调查，节省数小时时间。数千家全球公司使用Vanta实现证据收集自动化、统一风险管理并简化安全审核。访问Vanta.com/Lenny即可享受1000美元优惠。（05:18）：我想先问一个您前同事建议我问的问题。韦斯·考。我想您应该记得韦斯吧？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Of course. Wes and I sat in a room just the two of us for years.
turns.zh: 当然。韦斯和我多年来一直是只有我们两人共处一室的伙伴。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what she suggested I ask you, and this question I love, is she... I asked her, what did you learn most from Seth Godin working with him? And she immediately said, it's helping her build better taste and increase her standards, having really high standards. So I want to ask you first of all, just how do you know if you have good taste and high standards and then how do you build good taste and higher standards?
turns.zh: 所以她建议我问您的问题——我很喜欢这个问题——是她……我问她，从与赛斯·高汀合作中，你学到最多的是什么？她立刻回答，是帮助她建立更好的品味并提高标准，拥有非常高的标准。所以我想首先问您，您如何判断自己是否有良好的品味和高标准，然后又如何建立更好的品味和更高的标准？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Great question. Thank you, Wes. I define good taste as knowing what other people want just before they do. So if you're the only person who wants peanut butter covered licorice, you're entitled to eat peanut butter covered licorice, but you don't have good taste because everyone else thinks that's weird. And people, whether they're jazz musicians or fabric designers are seen as having good taste when they bring something to the world that the world didn't necessarily expect but is glad to see.
turns.zh: 好问题。谢谢你，韦斯。我把良好的品味定义为在别人还没意识到之前就知道他们想要什么。所以，如果你是唯一一个想吃花生酱包裹着甘草糖的人，你当然可以吃花生酱包裹着甘草糖，但你没有良好的品味，因为其他人都觉得这很奇怪。无论是爵士音乐家还是面料设计师，当他们为世界带来出乎意料却又令人欣喜的东西时，人们就会认为他们有良好的品味。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you find helps? So Wes learned from watching you that she realized, okay, my standards are not nearly as high as they could be. Other than working with you, maybe that's the answer is work with people like you that have really high standards. Just what do you find is most helpful in helping people build taste and also just increase their standards?
turns.zh: 你们觉得什么方法最有效？所以韦斯从观察你身上意识到，嗯，我的标准远远不够高。如果不算和你共事的话，也许关键在于要和像你这样拥有极高标准的人合作。那么，你们觉得帮助人们培养品味、提升标准最有效的方法是什么？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Standards, it's worth understanding what quality is and the people who listen to this podcast know better than most. Quality is not luxury. Quality is not perfection. Quality means meeting spec, and if you meet spec, you're done. If you don't think the spec is good enough, make a better spec. But if you meet spec, you're done. And so what it means to have high standards is that you relentlessly improve the spec in service of the people you're working with and for. (07:16): And what it doesn't mean is that you take something that meets spec and refuse to ship it because you're a perfectionist. That's hiding. And so what I learned at Spinnaker where I had my first job, real job as a product manager, was this idea that we weren't there to make perfect for us. We were there to delight the person who was buying the software. And our standards were untouchable. We said, "If that person, the one we're describing is delighted with what we shipped, it's good. And if they're not, it doesn't matter what kind of excuses we have." This is the opposite of what most people in this job do, which is they say, how do I please my boss? And if you're just doing your job, then don't expect to get rewarded for more than just doing your job because we can find lots of people who can just do your job.
turns.zh: 关于标准，值得理解的是什么是高质量，而听这个播客的人比大多数人都更清楚。高质量不是奢侈品，也不是完美主义。它意味着达到规格要求，如果达到了规格要求，就算完成了。如果你认为规格要求不够好，那就制定更高的规格。但如果达到了规格要求，就算完成了。所以拥有高标准意味着你为了与你共事和服务的人，不断提高标准。（07:16）但这并不意味着你要因为完美主义而拒绝交付符合规格的产品。这是在逃避责任。所以我在Spinnaker学到的，那是我第一份真正意义上的产品经理工作，是这样一个理念：我们不是为自己做完美产品，而是为了让购买我们软件的人满意。我们的标准是不可动摇的。我们说：“如果我们描述的那个用户对我们交付的产品满意，那就是好的。如果他们不满意，那就无所谓我们找什么借口。”这和大多数从事这份工作的人的做法正好相反，他们总是在想“我怎么才能取悦我的老板？”如果你只是在完成工作，那就别指望能得到超出完成工作的奖励，因为我们能找到很多能完成工作的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That reminds me of one of your other really powerful pieces of advice about how no matter your job, this is a tangent, but it really stuck with me once I read your advice here is no matter what job you have, you couldn't love it, enjoy it, be amazing at it, even if you're just like a waitress or whatever. Can you just talk through that? Because that's so powerful.
turns.zh: 这让我想起你另一个非常有力的建议，关于无论你的工作是什么——这有点跑题，但我读了你的建议后真的印象深刻——无论你做什么工作，你都无法热爱它、享受它、成为优秀的从业者，即使你只是个服务员之类的。你能详细说说吗？因为这太有力量了。

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Well, I think I got it from the late Reverend Martin Luther King Jr., and the idea is there's no perfect job. A friend of mine, Tim, is a famous jazz saxophonist and he's got to schlep from city to city, and he's got to play to half empty rooms and he is got to deal with this and deal with this. So you're never going to have unlimited artistic freedom. But what we all have is the ability to understand where the boundaries of our work lie and go there. (09:01): And if you're a barista and you've chosen to be a barista, maybe because it's the best thing you could get, well you're not going to get the next hour over again. So what would it be like to be the best barista in the world for an hour? Would that be worth it for you? Because I've had menial jobs in food service and I got to tell you, when the boss forces you to be mediocre and bored, there's no amount of money they can pay you to do that job. But if you're there and you have a chance to add delight to someone's day, you're doing that for you, not because you're getting paid.
turns.zh: 嗯，我想我从已故的马丁·路德·金牧师那里得到的启发是，没有完美的工作。我的朋友蒂姆是个著名的爵士萨克斯手，他得从一个城市辗转到另一个城市，在半空的房间里演奏，还得应对各种难题。所以你永远不会拥有无限的艺术自由。但我们都有能力理解工作的界限在哪里，并努力去触及它。（09:01）如果你是一名咖啡师，并且选择了这份工作，也许是因为这是你能找到的最好的工作，那么你就无法重来接下来的一个小时。那么，如果能在一小时内成为世界上最棒的咖啡师，那对你是值得的吗？因为我在餐饮服务行业做过卑微的工作，我可以告诉你，当老板强迫你平庸无聊时，再多的钱也无法让你愿意做这份工作。但如果你在那里，有机会为别人的一天增添乐趣，那就是为了你自己做的，而不是为了钱。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you could totally tell these people in the world when you go to a barista that just you can tell, just loves their job. I know imagine she knows this is not her career long-term, but she just embraces it and just has fun with it. There's so much power to that. On a different note, you mentioned that you were product manager, which I did not know. That's amazing. So most of the people listening to this podcast are product managers. They're either product managers, founders, people that want to be founders, and then people that work with product managers. So first of all, I guess could you just share that part of your life? Because I don't think people know that.
turns.zh:
还有，你完全能看得出来，当你去咖啡店时，那些员工显然热爱自己的工作。虽然我知道他们或许并未将这份工作视为长远的职业规划，但他们能全身心投入其中，享受其中的乐趣。这份热情本身就极具感染力。

另外，你提到自己曾担任产品经理，我之前并不知道这件事。真是了不起啊！听这个播客的大多数听众都是产品经理——他们要么本身就是产品经理，要么是创始人，或者渴望成为创始人，再不然就是与产品经理共事的人。所以首先，我想请你分享一下你作为产品经理的经历？因为我觉得大多数人对此并不了解。

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: All right. So the origin story could take all day, but I'm not going to tell the whole thing. I'm going to tell the part that I thought was normal that turned out to be the luckiest thing in the world. The summers between the two years of business school are very important to establish your career arc. I got a job at Spinnaker Software. Spinnaker invented educational computer games. I was the 30th employee. And the summer was spent doing assistant brand manager kind of stuff, going to meetings with the ad agency, writing copy. But at the end of the summer, they had a lovely going away party for me, because I was flying back to California. And then at the end, the president of the company, the chairman of the company and the head of marketing bring me into this side when they say, "We have a secret project, we want you to work for us while you're at business school and we're all going to pay you almost nothing." (10:52): "Okay, what's the secret project?" "We're going to do computer adventure games with illustrations and music based on science fiction novels, and we've already acquired the work of Ray Bradbury and Arthur C. Clarke." Now, I had read every science fiction book in the Clearfield Public Library from Asimov to Zelazny. This was a dream come true, but they thought my job was going to be make the packaging and run the ads. And what I discovered, first of all is that I couldn't really go back to business school. So I showed up hardly at all at Stanford and just took a lot of red eyes. But I discovered that the engineers, the development team, they had a lot of people vying for their time. And if I didn't figure out how to get them to give me way more than my fair share of development, I wasn't going to have any products to make next Christmas and then I was going to be out of a job. (11:46): And so I started a newsletter internally, I was one of the first people in the world to have desktop publishing because I was a beta tester for the Mac, and in it I would mention anybody in the engineering team who had worked on my project and I would say something good about them. And then I would print it out and put it in every single person's inner office mailbox. And within three months, four months, partly because the project was really good, 40 engineers were working for me and no one was reporting to me. And so I became the de facto product manager and that is when I learned marketing is the product. You don't make a product and then hand it to some marketing yahoo and say, go put a logo on this. That the product we made, and five in a row went gold, saved the company. Though product is why it worked. (12:38): And so I was supposed to know how to code but I didn't, but I could be in the room. The last month, RadioShack had bought how many units? 3000 stores times five times five, a lot of units. And if we had missed a date, they were going to cancel the order and the company would go bankrupt, and the software wasn't even close to done. And we didn't have any source control like we do now. There was no cloud, so it was all in my head. So I did not leave the office. I'm not exaggerating this, I did not leave the office for the last 22 days, slept for four hours a night upstairs, and if anyone had a question, I could tell them who to talk to. (13:19): That was so thrilling. It was so thrilling to make those decisions, to cajole this team, none of whom were in it for the money, to make something we were proud of. And then the stuff ships, everyone else goes home to sleep for a month, but I am the project manager and the marketing guy, so I got to stay at work. And the next day the phone rings and it's Herbie Hancock on the phone, the great jazz musician, and Herbie says, "The receptionist said you're the person in charge of Fahrenheit 451." And I said, "Herbie? I'm 24 years old, man. Herbie?" And he went on and on about how he had stayed up all night to play it and that he loved it.
turns.zh:
好吧，这个起源故事可以讲一整天，但我不会全盘托出。我只讲讲我原本以为很正常、结果却成了人生最大幸运的部分。商学院两年的暑假对职业生涯规划至关重要。我当时在斯皮纳克软件公司工作，该公司专注于教育类电脑游戏开发。我是第30位员工。那个夏天，我主要做助理品牌经理之类的工作，参加广告公司会议，撰写宣传文案。但暑假结束时，公司为我举办了一场欢送派对，因为我要飞回加州了。临行前，公司总裁、董事长和市场部主管把我拉到一边说：“我们有个秘密项目，希望你能在商学院期间为我们工作，而且报酬微薄。”（10:52）“好吧，这个秘密项目是什么？”  “我们要基于科幻小说改编带有插图和音乐的冒险游戏，目前已获得雷·布拉德伯里和阿瑟·C·克拉克的授权。” 当时我读遍了克利尔菲尔德公共图书馆里从阿西莫夫到泽拉兹尼的所有科幻书籍。这简直是梦想成真，但他们以为我的工作只是包装设计和广告策划。结果我发现，自己根本回不去商学院了。我在斯坦福大学几乎不露面，还挂了不少科目。但我发现工程师团队争分夺秒地开发产品，如果我不能让他们投入远超应有的精力，我明年圣诞节就失业了。（11:46）于是我创办了内部通讯，作为全球首批使用桌面排版的用户（因为我是Mac测试员），我在通讯中提及参与项目的工程师，并给予他们积极评价。然后把文件打印出来，放进每个人的办公室信箱。三四个月后，部分归功于项目质量上乘，40名工程师为我效力却无需向我汇报。我成了事实上的产品经理，那时我领悟到营销就是产品本身。你不能先做产品，再交给营销人员贴个标签了事。我们亲手打造的产品，连续五款大获成功，拯救了公司。产品本身才是成功的关键。（12:38）当时我本该懂编程却一窍不通，但我能在场监督。最后一个月RadioShack要采购多少设备？3000家门店，每家五个套装，数量庞大。若延期交货，公司必定破产，而软件还远未完成。更别提当时根本没有源代码控制系统。所有数据都存在我脑海中，所以最后22天我足不出户，日夜颠倒，楼上睡觉，楼下解答问题。（13:19）那种感觉太激动人心了。能亲自做决策，凝聚那些不为金钱而来的团队，打造出令自己骄傲的产品。产品上线后，其他人回家睡大觉，而我仍是项目经理兼营销总监。
天哪，所以我只能继续工作了。第二天电话响了，接电话的是赫比·汉考克——那位伟大的爵士音乐家。他说：“接待员说你负责《华氏451》这部作品。”我说：“赫比？我才24岁啊，老兄。赫比？” 他接着说自己整晚都在玩这款游戏，并且非常喜欢它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how natural of a product manager you were in these things you shared of just thinking everyone deflecting credit and all these things. It's sign of a great PM. Along these lines, I wanted to ask actually, so you're a PM early on. Now, you obviously spend a lot of time marketing. I know you're saying there's obviously a strong connection between the two, but is there anything you find that people building the product most often miss or misunderstand that just annoys you or do you think they need to hear?
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你在分享的这些内容中展现出的产品经理特质——自然而然、毫不做作。比如你提到大家都在推诿功劳之类的，这正是优秀产品经理的典型表现。顺便说一句，你现在才刚入行产品经理，但显然已经花了大量时间在市场营销上。我知道你说两者之间有紧密联系，但有没有一些产品开发者常犯的错误或误解，让你觉得特别恼火，或者你认为他们亟需纠正？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Maybe I got seven, but I'll try to do them off the top of my head. The first one is this, empathy is not about kindness and empathy is not an option. This is something that you are making for other people. So the whole idea of RTFM, read the manual, I'm angry at you. If you're saying that to your customers, you made a mistake, they did not make a mistake. (14:49): The second one is that the thing about projects is when you run out of time and you run out of money, the project is over. Don't run out of time, don't run out of money. Good intentions are no reason for an extension. The professional doesn't ask for an extension because the professional understands that things you didn't expect are going to happen. That's part of the deal. (15:14): And I guess the third one would be for software, particularly software as a service, if you don't build the network effect into what you are making, you are almost certainly going to fail. You cannot hope that Apple's going to pick you, promote you, and magically have you be successful. The question is, will this work better for my users if they tell other people about it? And if the answer is no, then why would they tell other people about it? And if they don't tell other people about it, no one's going to hear about it. But if the answer is yes, then your marketing problems pretty much solved.
turns.zh:
或许我总结了七条，但我尽量凭记忆说出来。第一条是，同理心不等于善良，也不是可选项。这是为他人打造的产品。所以“去读手册”这种说法让我很生气。如果你对客户这么说，那你就错了，错的是他们。（14:49）  
第二条是，项目管理的核心是时间和资金一旦耗尽，项目就结束了。别让时间和资金耗尽。善意不是延期理由。专业人士不会要求延期，因为他们明白意外情况会发生，这就是规则的一部分。（15:14）  
第三条是，软件产品尤其是SaaS产品，如果不内置网络效应，几乎注定失败。别指望苹果会青睐你、推广你然后奇迹般让你成功。关键问题是：如果用户把产品推荐给别人，体验会更好吗？如果答案否定，他们为什么要推荐？如果不推荐，就没人知道。但如果答案肯定，那你的营销问题就基本解决了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like each of these is its own book that we could talk through. And I want to come back to this last point and how it relates to the purple cow. I want to spend a little time there, but first I'm going to ask a marketing question. So before you came on, I asked on Twitter, what should I ask Seth Godin? He's coming on my podcast. I got a flood of suggestions. The most recurring theme actually had to do with AI. Actually the co-founder of Intercom asked this question and it echoes what many people are wondering. So his question is how do you think all these new AI companies build brands to distinguish and differentiate themselves in a world that's increasingly filled with AI companies, AI products, AI content?
turns.zh: 我觉得每条都值得单独成册深入探讨。我想回归到最后一点，以及它与“紫牛”理论的关联。我想花点时间深入探讨，但首先我要问个营销问题。你来之前我在推特上征集问题，应该问塞斯·戈丁什么。他要来我的播客，我收到了大量建议。其中最热门的话题是AI。Intercom的联合创始人提了一个问题，呼应了许多人的疑惑：在AI公司、AI产品、AI内容日益泛滥的世界里，新兴AI公司如何通过品牌建设实现差异化？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Well, the first question is what's a brand? Because it's not a logo. A brand is a promise. It's what do I expect from you. It's would I miss you if you were gone. And Hyatt Hotels has a logo, Nike has a brand. The way we know this is if Nike opened a hotel, we'd know what it would be like. But if Hyatt decided to make sneakers, we have no clue. They might be comfortable, but that's all we would know. And so if you want to build a brand, you got to stand for something and you got to say what you don't do. And the second thing is AI very soon is going to stop being a feature the same way electricity is not a feature. That lots and lots of things run on electricity, but they're not electricity companies. They just happen to use electricity. (17:13): So what AI companies and all companies need to do is say, what's in this for the user? What promise do I want to make? A difficult promise, a remarkable promise. And then how do I keep it? So making absurd promises might work at the VC level, but it doesn't work when you're talking to consumers because you can only break that promise one time. And so to wrap up the brand part, airlines don't have brands and airlines don't have loyalty. And the way we know this is that the only reason people stick with an airline is for the points, which is bribery. Loyalty is would you pay extra to stick with this? And if you wouldn't pay extra, then the brand has no value.
turns.zh: 嗯，首先第一个问题是，什么是品牌？因为它不是一个标志。品牌是一个承诺。它是用户对你的期望。它是当你离开时别人会不会想念你。而凯悦酒店有标志，耐克有品牌。我们能分辨出来是因为，如果耐克开一家酒店，我们能猜到它的样子。但如果凯悦决定做运动鞋，我们就完全没概念了。它们可能会很舒适，但仅此而已。所以如果你想打造一个品牌，就必须代表某种价值观，还要明确自己不做什么。第二点是，人工智能很快就不再是产品特性了，就像电力不再是产品特性一样。很多东西都依赖电力，但电力公司可不是电力本身。（17:13）所以人工智能公司和所有企业需要做的是：对用户有什么价值？我想传递什么样的承诺？一个高远的承诺，一个非凡的承诺。然后如何兑现它？在风投层面说些夸大其词的承诺或许行得通，但对消费者来说就不管用了，因为你只能违背一次承诺。所以总结品牌部分，航空公司没有品牌，也没有忠诚度。这一点我们能看出来，人们选择一家航空公司唯一的原因就是积分，而积分就是贿赂。忠诚度应该是你愿意为此多付钱吗？如果不愿意多付钱，那品牌就没有价值了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this phrase, make a promise and keep it. And the AI element, that raises the bar because many more promises are being made, fewer promises are probably being kept. So is the advice there, continue making an ambitious promise and then the key is actually deliver on that and that's what builds you brand?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这句话，许下承诺并兑现它。人工智能部分把标准提得很高，因为现在许下的承诺更多了，但兑现的却更少了。所以建议是继续许下一个雄心勃勃的承诺，然后关键在于真正兑现它，这才能建立你的品牌？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Yeah. I have a very emotional connection to Claude.ai. I think they have a brand. ChatGPT's reputation with me is not good because it regularly over promises and under delivers and it does it without kindness or humility. Whereas Claude, I don't know how they did it, at least in my experience, brings kindness and humility. So when it doesn't know, it's very clear and it's not lazy and it's not angry at me. And so I happily pay extra for Claude because it has a brand. Whereas ChatGPT for me is just a tool that I use if I have no other options.
turns.zh: 是的。我对Claude.ai有很深的感情。我觉得他们有品牌。ChatGPT在我心中的声誉不佳，因为它经常夸大其词却兑现不足，而且态度既不友善也不谦逊。而Claude，我不知道他们是怎么做到的，至少在我的体验中，它带着友善和谦逊。所以当它不知道答案时，会很明确，不会敷衍了事，也不会对我发脾气。所以我很乐意为Claude多付钱，因为它有品牌。而ChatGPT对我来说只是一个工具，如果没有其他选择时才会用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the Anthropic/Claude's billboards. "We're the ones without the drama." The AI company without the drama. I was going to save this to the end, but let's actually talk about it. So you mentioned somewhere that you actually use Claude to help you write this book and refine the book, which I think is going to increasingly happen. Could you just share that process of how you did that? What did you do that might be helpful to people to help you write this book?
turns.zh: 我喜欢Anthropic/Claude的广告牌。“我们是没有戏剧性的。”这家没有戏剧化的AI公司。我本来想把这个留到最后，但还是说说吧。你之前提到过你用Claude来帮助你写这本书和润色书稿，我觉得这种情况会越来越多。你能分享一下你是如何操作的吗？你做了哪些有助于写书的操作？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Well, to be clear about my brand promise, because it's true, every word that has my name on it, I wrote. Every blog post, every book. I don't have a team. This is my whole staff is me. What I did with Claude and which I encourage people to do in the book is I would upload a list of four things and say, what did I miss? And it would suggest three things to complete the list. And often they would be things I hadn't thought of. And then I could go write about that or I would upload a couple chapters and I would say, what are the claims I'm making here that you don't think that I'm sustaining? And it became this patient editor that is so hard to find in the real world because editors aren't paid enough and given enough time to do their job right. And what I find is if I have a sentence that doesn't sound enough like me, I can ask Claude to help me figure out why that's true.
turns.zh: 嗯，关于我的品牌承诺，我得说清楚一点，因为这是事实——凡是署有我名字的内容，无论是博客文章还是书籍，都是我亲自撰写的。我没有团队，整个团队就是我自己。和克劳德一起尝试的方法（我也在书中鼓励读者这样做）是，我会上传一个四项任务清单，然后问：“我遗漏了什么？” 系统会给出三项建议来完善清单。很多时候，这些建议都是我之前没想到的。之后我会写下相关内容，或者上传几章内容，问读者：“我在这里提出的主张，你觉得我没有做到吗？” 这就像有个耐心的编辑——在现实世界中，这种编辑很难找到，因为他们的报酬太低，工作时间又不足。而我发现，如果有一句话听起来不像我的风格，我就能让克劳德帮我找出原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that tactic of using it to figure out what you missed. I feel like you agree with this. I find that when I write, part of it is I'm putting an idea out there. I want to see what I got wrong and what I missed. And I like that you basically skip that step and don't put it out and just make the thing you put out actually better.
turns.zh: 我喜欢用这种方法来发现自己遗漏的部分。我觉得你也认同这种做法。我发现自己写作时，部分原因是想把一个想法呈现出来，看看自己哪里做得不对，有什么遗漏的。而你基本上跳过了这个步骤，不把内容发布出去，而是直接把写好的内容做得更好。

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Well, the thing about blogging every day is at first it felt like how am I going to keep up? But once I could build a queue because I didn't want my streak to end-
turns.zh: 嗯，每天写博客一开始让我觉得怎么才能坚持下去？但后来我建立了一个内容队列，因为不想让自己的连胜纪录中断——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How long is the streak at this point, by the way?
turns.zh: 顺便问一下，现在你的连胜纪录持续多久了？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Post number 10,000 comes out at the beginning of 2025.
turns.zh: 2025年初会迎来第10000篇博文。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God. In a row.
turns.zh: 天哪。连续不间断的。

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: In a row. Some days there were two. But what I found as I got a little bit of a queue is that I would feel bad because I had something to say, but I couldn't because there was already one in the queue. So I shifted from I have to write something to I get to write something. And now because I've taken the pressure off, I have time to rewrite it because I don't have a shortage of ideas for tomorrow. I have extra ones.
turns.zh: 连续不间断的。有时候一天会写两篇。但当我积累了一些内容队列后，我发现自己会因为有话想说却被队列里的内容占据而感到沮丧。所以我从“必须写点什么”转变为“有机会写点什么”。现在压力减轻了，我有时间重写内容，因为明天不会缺少灵感，我还有额外的素材。

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Yeah. And for a product person, these are the critical choices and you probably have glossed over them. You have probably assumed it's a given and you've sacrificed your agency over the four most important things you should be choosing. So the first one is picking your customers. If your motto is you can pick anyone and we're anyone, if your hope is that you have to win SEO to get anything, you're not going to succeed. When you choose your smallest viable audience, what language they speak, how much money they have, what problem they're trying to solve, what their technical facility is, whether they're short-tempered, whether they're kind, whether they're going to stick with you, you have chosen everything that's going to go into the product and what your future is going to be like. And so the Humane Pin people, whatever it was called, made a mistake when they picked their customers because they showed up like they had a finished Apple-quality product and they were trying to appeal to the kind of people that would buy on pre-order a finished Apple quality product. (24:40): When they shipped something that wasn't that, and they knew it wasn't that, they're doomed. Whereas if you say, here we are in Product Hunt, we're only looking for 400 people. We're looking for people who like the Raspberry Pi. Who wants to wonk with this thing? Now you can dance and you can have all these other things happen because you picked a different customer. If you decide to be a wedding photographer in the Hamptons, well you better expect to have some very spoiled, cranky brides and grooms, and grooms and grooms, and brides and brides, that you have to deal with because you picked your customers. Okay, so then the second one which comes with that is who's your competition? Because if you're competing against Walmart, why are you surprised that they keep lowering their prices? That's what Walmart does, right? That way you decide which space that you're going to operate in. You've built an enormous set of boundaries around what you do. (25:36): The third one is validation. If you are trying to please your boss, that's what you're going to do. If on the other hand, you can have one difficult conversation with your boss and say, can we agree that I'm not trying to match your taste, I'm trying to match the taste of these 400 people that we've agreed are our customers? Every other meeting is going to go way better from now on because you've made it clear who you're trying to please. (26:01): And the last one, choose your distribution matters a lot in the software business. For example, a video game, which is where I started, we were in Target and Lechmere and mass merchants. Our competitors were in Ziploc bags in computer stores. Well, when something like Steam shows up, when something like downloadable shareware shows up, everything about your product changes. So again, these four things are choices, and if you're glossing over them it's because you're afraid.
turns.zh:
是啊。对于产品经理来说，这些都是至关重要的决策，而你很可能忽视了它们。你可能认为这些都是理所当然的，却为此牺牲了自主权。首先是选择客户群体。如果你的口号是“我们面向所有人”，或者希望通过SEO优化获取市场份额，那你注定不会成功。当你锁定最小可行客户群体时，比如他们的语言偏好、消费能力、待解决的问题、技术水平、性格特质，以及客户的忠诚度时，你就决定了产品核心属性和未来发展方向。

拿Humane Pin（原名）来说。他们在选择客户群体时就犯了错误，因为他们推出了看似苹果级别的产品，却试图吸引那些愿意预购这种产品的人。结果当产品实际质量不达标时，他们注定失败。而如果你在Product Hunt上只招募400名用户，目标客户是喜欢树莓派（Raspberry Pi）的人，那么你就能创造出完全不同的产品生态。再比如，如果你决定成为汉普顿地区的婚礼摄影师，那你最好做好面对挑剔的新人客户的准备，因为客户的选择决定了你的竞争空间。

第二个关键点是竞争对手分析。如果你与沃尔玛竞争，就别惊讶他们不断压低价格——这就是沃尔玛的策略。通过界定清晰的竞争边界，你能有效构建壁垒。第三点是验证策略。如果你只想取悦老板，那你的方向注定偏离。如果你能与老板进行一次艰难对话，坦言“我们不追求迎合你的审美，而是这400位客户的需求”，那么后续所有会议都会更加顺畅。

最后一点，分销渠道选择在软件行业至关重要。比如我早期从事的视频游戏行业，我们的目标客户是塔吉特（Target）、Lechmere等大型零售商，而竞争对手的产品却只能装在ziploc袋子里在电脑城销售。Steam平台和可下载共享软件的出现彻底重构了整个产业链。这些决策环环相扣，忽视其中任何一环都可能导致失败。

需要强调的是，这些决策并非可以随意更改。例如，调整分销策略必须与产品定位相契合。关键在于，确保产品团队清晰理解分销策略与目标客户的深度关联。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think it's important to note, it's not like you can just change these at will and just like, okay, cool, we'll change your distribution. These are intertwined. But the important point here that I hear is just make sure the product you're building understands this is how you'll be distributed. This is who you're selling to.
turns.zh: 我认为重要的是，要认识到这些决策并非随意更改。比如，调整分销策略并非易事，这些因素相互交织。但我从中领悟到的核心要义是：确保你正在打造的产品清晰理解其分销路径和目标客户群体。

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, so a friend just sent me a business plan. They're making a food product and they're saying, we're going to distribute on Shopify and we're also going to sell to businesses, airports, hotels, and people who need to sell the food. I'm like, there's only two of you. No, that's not what your business... You got to pick, today, before you even turn the page, who are you for and who are you not for?
turns.zh: 是啊，我是说，有个朋友刚给我发了一份商业计划书。他们要生产一种食品产品，还说要在Shopify上分销，同时向企业、机场、酒店以及需要销售食品的人群销售。我就想，咱们才两个人啊。这可不是你的业务重点……你今天就得选，翻开第一页之前，先想清楚你的目标客户是谁，不然根本没法开展业务！

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along the lines of picking your customer reminds me, a friend of mine started a company selling a product to real estate agents and she just warned me, be careful who you're selling to because you're going to be spending a lot of time with these people. Make sure you're ready to be doing that.
turns.zh: 说到选择目标客户，这让我想起我一个朋友。她创办了一家面向房地产经纪人的产品销售公司，还特别提醒我：小心选择合作对象，因为你得长期与这些人打交道。要确保自己能应付得来。

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: One of my very first books was a advertising supported directory paid for by law firms. This is not something I want to recommend to anybody.
turns.zh: 我最早写的书之一是为律师事务所付费制作的广告支持目录。我可不想向任何人推荐这种模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another great nugget from the book that really stood out to me is this idea of tension. The importance of tension. You basically talk about how a great strategy has tension at the center of it. Why is tension so important to a good strategy?
turns.zh: 书中另一个让我印象深刻的核心观点是"张力"。张力的重要性不言而喻。你说一个优秀的战略，其核心必定存在张力。为什么张力对一个好战略如此重要？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Okay, so let's agree that tension and stress aren't the same thing. Stress is generally not good. Stress is two things at the same time, I want to leave, I need to stay. Right? I hate my boss, but I need this job. That's stress. Don't look for stress. Tension is at the heart of every art form and every innovation. Tension is it might not work. Tension is da-da-da-na-na, and the other person says, da-da. Because they need to finish the sentence. (28:23): So what we do when we launch a new product is we say, we have this thing that can do X, and now the person is imagining what their life might be like if that were true. If they fall in love with that possibility, now there's tension. Did you tell the truth? Is it going to work for them? And when I was a kid, PF Flyers were the sneaker to get, this was before Nike. And the promise of PF Flyers was that they would finally make you fast enough to run away from the bully. And I remember 10 years old walking into that shoe store and there was real tension in my head because I needed to get away from that bully, and I was keeping the PF Flyers people to their promise, and they didn't tell the truth.
turns.zh: 好吧，让我们先承认张力和压力不是一回事。压力通常不是什么好东西。压力就是当你同时面临两种选择：想离开却又不得不留下。就像我讨厌老板却又需要这份工作，这就是压力。但别刻意追求压力。张力是每种艺术形式和每项创新的核心。张力意味着可能失败。张力就是达达达娜娜，而对方回应达达达。（28:23）举个例子，我们推出新产品时会说：我们的产品能做到X，现在用户正在想象如果真能实现会是什么样子。如果他们爱上了这个可能性，就产生了张力。你说实话了吗？这对他们管用吗？我小时候，PF Flyers鞋子是必备之选，那时候还没耐克。PF Flyers的承诺是能让你跑得足够快，摆脱霸凌者。我记得10岁那年走进鞋店时，脑海里满是紧张感，因为我急着逃离霸凌者，而PF Flyers团队却没兑现承诺。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It comes back to your point about not delivering on the promise that you make to build-
turns.zh: 这又回到了你提到的不能兑现承诺的问题……

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... A great brand, right? Okay, I want to take a little tangent into Purple Cow territory. I have your book right here, by the way. I have many of your books in the back, but I don't want to make my library... Oh, what is that? A milk carton?
turns.zh: ……一个伟大的品牌，对吧？好吧，我想稍微偏题一下，聊聊《紫牛》。我顺便说一句，我有你的书。书房里还有好几本，但不想把书架堆得太高……哦，那是什么？牛奶纸箱？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: This is the first 10,000 copies came in milk carton.
turns.zh: 第一批1万本就是用牛奶纸箱包装的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man, I missed out on that. Was there any purple milk inside? What color is a purple cow's milk? We'll never know. We'll never know. I know you've talked about this concept a gazillion times. I feel like still people don't actually... Many people haven't heard it. Many people don't truly understand it, and it's the thing that I reference most of your piece of advice. Could you spend a little time just chatting about this topic of the Purple Cow, the importance of being remarkable?
turns.zh: 天哪，我错过了那个机会。里面有紫色的牛奶吗？紫牛的奶是什么颜色？永远不得而知了。永远不得而知了。我知道你反复强调这个概念无数次。但感觉还是很多人没真正理解。这也是我最常参考你的建议的一点。能不能花点时间聊聊紫牛这个话题，聊聊成为非凡存在的重要性？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Okay, so let's start with Steve Blank. I'm sure you've talked about his idea of customer traction. The single best way to tell if a startup's got any hope whatsoever is do the people who engage with you stick around? Do they come back for more? The second piece is, do they tell their friends? And if they tell their friends, what do they say? The word remarkable means worth making a remark about. So I'm not talking about coming up with some viral video that's ridiculous in its gimmickry. I'm saying if you make something where the person's life gets better if they talk about you and you know in advance what you want them to say, then they are more likely to say it. So Marissa Mayer probably created more stock market value than any other product manager I can think of. And the way she did it was there weren't very many people at Google, but she was the one who said, "No, you can't put another button on the homepage. There are only going to be two buttons on the homepage." And over and over and again. (31:04): At the time I was at Yahoo. Yahoo had the chance to buy Google for $10 million while I was there. That's a whole interesting story. But Yahoo had 183 links on the homepage and Google had two. And the statement built into that is we are making you a promise, and the promise is we are smart enough to take you where you want to go without you spending a lot of time browsing through 183 links. Tell us what you want and we'll take you there. And so I was a tech-forward person, and if a friend came to me lost on the internet, confused about something, I'd just send them to Google because I knew they wouldn't come back to me for more help, because okay, fine, they're gone. It's going to work. That's what to say about Google at its launch is, hey, just type in what you want and you'll find it. They built that into the product. That makes it remarkable because I wanted to tell other people about that because it would raise my status as a tech innovator.
turns.zh: 好的，首先我们来谈谈史蒂夫·布兰克。我相信你们都听说过他提出的客户牵引力（customer traction）理念。判断一家初创公司是否有成功希望的最佳方法，就是看看与你互动的人是否会留下来？他们会不会再来光顾？第二个关键点是，他们会不会把你推荐给朋友？如果他们推荐了，又会怎么说？‘非凡’这个词意味着值得人们津津乐道。所以我不是说要制作那种靠噱头吸引眼球的病毒视频。我是说，如果你能开发出这样一种产品——当用户谈论你时，他们的生活会因此变得更美好，而且你提前就知道他们会怎么说——那么他们就更有可能去传播。马丽莎·梅耶尔（Marissa Mayer）创造的股票市值，可能比我能想到的任何其他产品经理都要多。她在谷歌的策略是：当时谷歌团队规模不大，但她坚持说：“不行，你不能在主页上再加一个按钮。主页上只能有两个按钮。”一次又一次地强调。（31:04）：当时我在雅虎。雅虎曾有机会以1000万美元收购谷歌，但我离开雅虎后谷歌已经上市了。这是一个很有趣的故事。雅虎的主页有183个链接，而谷歌只有两个。谷歌传递的核心理念是：我们向你承诺，我们足够聪明，能带你去你想去的地方，而无需你耗费大量时间浏览183个链接。告诉我们你想要什么，我们就能带你去那里。我曾是个科技前沿人士，如果朋友在网上迷路或遇到难题，我会直接让他们用谷歌搜索，因为我知道他们不会再回来找我求助，因为好吧，他们走了。这就是谷歌刚推出时要传达的信息：嘿，只要输入你想要的，就能找到。谷歌把这一理念融入了产品。这很了不起，因为我想把它推荐给其他人，因为这能提升我作为科技创新者的地位。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the implication here, and you talked about this, is that most likely the way you will win is word of mouth. It's hard to win with paid ads. It's hard to win with sales teams unless you're building B2B software. What you need to focus on is how to build something people tell their friends about. And the core of that is being remarkable. And I love just the way you break it down. Being remarkable is being something people remark about.
turns.zh: 这里暗含的意思，你也提到过，那就是你最有可能通过口碑取胜。靠付费广告很难成功。除非你开发的是B2B软件，否则很难靠销售团队取胜。你需要专注于如何开发出让人们愿意推荐给朋友的产品。而核心在于做到非凡。我很欣赏你把这个概念拆解得如此透彻。非凡意味着值得人们津津乐道。

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Yeah, and if you think it's just for small companies, that's how Microsoft beat WordPerfect, because Microsoft Word was the format you needed your coworkers to work in if you were using a modern computer, because if they insisted on using WordPerfect, then you were stuck with WordPerfect. Whereas they had a migration path and once you migrated, you didn't go back. So again, it's in my interest to insist you use Word. So I did.
turns.zh: 是的，如果你认为这只适用于小公司，那微软击败WordPerfect就是个例子。因为微软Word是现代电脑用户必须使用的格式，而如果他们坚持用WordPerfect，那就只能被困在WordPerfect里了。而微软提供了迁移路径，一旦迁移就不会回头。所以再说一次，坚持让用户用Word符合我的利益。所以我这么做了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This point about Mercer Mayer of doing this thing that was controversial, it comes back to your point of creating tension. It feels like it created tension both with visitors and internally. There's also these quotes that I have here that are along these lines that you've said in the past, I don't think they're in this book. If it scares you, it might be a good thing to try. And safety is risky. Is there anything you want to say there?
turns.zh: 关于梅耶尔做那些引发争议的事，这里又回到了你提到的制造紧张感的观点。看起来这在用户和内部都制造了紧张感。我这里还有一些你过去说过的话的引语，我觉得书里没有提到这些。假如它吓到你了，或许值得一试。安全就是冒险。你对此有什么想说的吗？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Well, so one of the things I talk about in the book is that systems are everywhere we look and they're largely invisible, taken for granted. I spend time with high school seniors talking about college. They don't see the college industrial complex. They just think it's normal, because that's what it is to grow up in the suburbs. And what systems do to protect themselves is they invent culture. Culture is the way things are around here. And so if you think something is scary, that's probably because the system wants you to think that. (33:57): And so you shouldn't do something foolhardy. You shouldn't be fearless. But what you should do is think about why does it scare me to do this? What system will be offended if I do that? Am I trying to work with the system or am I leveraged enough to help change the system? And so the first people who put up downloadable software, all the feedback was, you can't do that. It'll be pirated. You'll never make a penny. Okay. That might happen, and I can see why that feels scary, but I could also see why the dominant system of software distribution doesn't want me to even experiment with this. But I only worked on the software for five months, let's try it, because if it doesn't work and it gets pirated, I'll just have to make new software. It's okay.
turns.zh: 嗯，我在书中提到的观点之一是，系统无处不在，却又大多被人们视而不见、认为理所当然。我曾和高中毕业生们谈论大学，他们看不到大学这个产业链。他们只是觉得这很正常，因为这就是在郊区成长的常态。而系统为了自我保护，会虚构出一种文化——这种文化就是现状。所以如果你觉得某件事令人恐惧，那很可能是系统希望你这么想。（33:57）所以你不应该鲁莽行事，不应该无所畏惧。但你应该思考：为什么我会害怕做这件事？如果我这么做，哪个系统会感到被冒犯？我是想顺应现有系统，还是已经拥有足够的力量去改变它？最初发布可下载软件的人得到的反馈都是：你不能这么做，软件会被盗版的，你永远赚不到钱。好吧，这种情况可能会发生，我能理解这让人感到害怕，但我也能理解主流的软件分发系统为什么不希望我去尝试。但我只花了五个月时间开发这个软件，试试看吧，因为即使失败了被盗版，我再做新的软件就行了。没关系。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting, the opposite of that was also true with Salesforce. Their whole pitch was no software. It's all in the cloud. Once that became the system, that became the tension and the risky move.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，Salesforce的情况正好相反。他们当时宣传的重点是无需安装软件，一切都在云端。一旦这成为行业标准，问题就出现了，这反而成了一个充满风险的突破。

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you have this quote, actually. I want to spend more time on the system concept because it's so core to the book, and so core to your advice for how to be better, you have this actual quote. "What does it mean to be a strategic thinker? It means to see the system." What else can you share about it just for people that are trying to become better strategically, to understand what you mean when you talk about the system, how to see the system?
turns.zh: 你提到了这句话。我想多花点时间讲讲系统这个概念，因为它对本书至关重要，也是你给出如何变得更优秀的建议的核心。书中有一句话：“成为战略思考者意味着什么？意味着看清系统。” 对于那些想在战略思维上有所提升的人，你能否再多讲讲，解释一下你所说的‘系统’是什么意思，以及如何看清这个系统？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: We have to invent systems anytime we engage with other human beings, because interoperability is essential. There's a system for how we greet other people in our culture. You shake hands, right hand to right hand. And just show up sometime and give the Vulcan salute instead and watch what happens. It's very awkward because we just needed to get this over with and now that's part of the system. And so systems serve a valuable function until they don't, because then the system starts doing things to support itself, to reinforce itself. So for example, there is a system that says we should interview people for jobs. And the most successful interviews are people where they show that they are like us, they look like us, they went to schools like us, they have privilege and background like us. That is toxic, because it diminishes not just diversity, but our ability to put real talent on the team. (36:19): And if you don't see that system and name that system, you're going to keep doing what you were doing. And I was talking to someone yesterday who said they had been working with a company and the last four people that they had hired had been captain of their Ivy League tennis team. Well, clearly there's a pattern here and it's being reinforced by people who don't want to get in trouble, but the system's not helping them. And so yes, we need the metric system and we need the zip code system. Those keep working really well. But if you are trying to show up in a place where dominant players don't want you to succeed, you're going to have to find something in the system that gives you a chance to change the rules.
turns.zh:
每当我们与他人互动时，都必须构建新的体系，因为互操作性至关重要。我们的文化中存在问候他人的固定模式——通常是右手与右手相握。但如果你突然出现，用瓦肯人的敬礼手势打招呼，看看会发生什么。这种情况会令人尴尬，因为我们只是想完成这项任务，而现在这已成为体系的一部分。体系在有效运作时发挥着重要作用，但当它开始自我强化、自我复制时，问题就出现了。比如，招聘面试的体系就存在偏见——成功的面试者往往与我们相似：出身名校、拥有相似背景、享有特权。这种偏见既损害了多样性，也阻碍了真正人才的加入。

（36:19）如果你不审视并命名这种体系，就会继续沿袭旧习。我昨天与某人交谈，他们透露在一家公司，过去四位新入职者都是常春藤盟校网球队队长。显然存在一种模式，而那些不愿惹麻烦的人在强化这种模式，但体系本身并无助益。因此，我们需要公制计量单位和邮政编码系统——这些体系至今仍行之有效。但当你试图进入一个不欢迎你的主流体系时，就必须在体系中寻找能改变规则的机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This metaphor that I love that's along these lines of better waves make better surfers, that a lot of your success is driven by choosing the wave versus the skills that you have. Can you just talk about that?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这样一个比喻：好浪才能造就好冲浪者，你的成功很大程度上取决于如何选择浪况，而非自身技能。你能否谈谈这一观点？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Yeah. So it's surprisingly profound. I don't know where I came up with it, but when I see people who are great at surfing, they're almost always on good waves. And my son who surfs a lot, I have noticed, passes up waves that other people might take waiting for the right wave because he knows he will be able to surf it better. So when you think about which company you're signing up to bring software from, which people you're willing to put on the key roles, are you willing to wait for the superstar who's going to change things or are you in so much of a hurry to make an imaginary deadline that you're going to ship mediocre work? Because all mediocre means is average. And so if you don't want to be mediocre, you better do something different than the other people are doing. Otherwise, you're going to get what the other people are getting.
turns.zh: 是的，这个比喻很深刻。我也不知道自己从何处得到灵感，但当我观察那些冲浪高手时，他们几乎总能驾驭优质浪况。我儿子经常冲浪，我发现他会放弃别人认为值得尝试的浪况，专等最佳时机，因为他知道自己能冲得更好。那么，当你选择合作伙伴开发软件，或决定让哪些人担任关键角色时，你是愿意等待能改变局面的超级巨星，还是急于赶上虚构的截止日期而交出平庸之作？因为平庸不过是平均水平。若你不甘平庸，就必须采取与众不同的做法，否则只能收获他人所得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As you talk about this, I'm thinking about, I don't know if you saw Jaguar's rebrand and their whole launch. And it feels like it's been rejected by the system. Any thoughts on that? Maybe what they got wrong or maybe it was genius?
turns.zh: 听你谈到这些，我想到了，不知道你是否关注过捷豹的品牌重塑和新品发布。感觉它被体系拒绝了。对此你有什么看法？或许他们做错了什么，或许这就是天才之举？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Okay, so you've picked a topic that I really like to talk about. Jaguar did not rebrand, Jaguar re-logo-ed. And the logo might be a sign that they're trying to rebrand and make a different promise, and they're switching to all electric, which I'm in favor of. But they made, I think, a very significant error, which is if you're going to start a car company, a hundred million or a billion dollars are going to get spent earning trust from people who never heard of you. If you're starting with one of the most iconic and beautiful and beloved car brands that has the luxury of having almost no cars in the world that could undermine what you want it to stand for going forward, it's perfect. Own that, that's brilliant. And to walk away from that so that you could please some art director, I don't understand why you think you're rebranding when you just put a logo on that undermines many of the awareness assets you already had going for you.
turns.zh: 好吧，你选了一个我特别喜欢谈论的话题。捷豹不是重塑品牌，而是更换了标志。新标志或许暗示着他们试图重塑品牌形象，树立新的品牌承诺，同时向全电动化转型——我对此举持赞同态度。但我认为他们犯了一个严重错误：如果要创立一家汽车公司，动辄花费数亿美元去赢得那些从未听说过你的品牌的消费者信任固然重要。但若你要接手一个全球知名的、极具美感且深受大众喜爱的汽车品牌——这个品牌几乎没有竞争对手能威胁到其品牌核心价值，那就堪称完美。抓住这一点才是明智之举。然而他们却为了取悦某位艺术总监而舍弃了原有品牌形象，这简直令人费解——当你试图重塑品牌时，却用一个损害品牌资产的新标志来取代原有形象，这实在是得不偿失。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like they got very, very controversial. They went against the status quo more maybe than they should. I don't know. What would you have done if you were them?
turns.zh: 感觉他们这次引发了巨大争议。他们打破常规的程度或许超出了应有的限度。说实话，如果换作你我，面对同样的挑战会怎么做？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: You may recall when the International House of Pancakes decided to falsely announce they were changing their name to the International House of Burgers and made a new logo, because they wanted buzz. This is a Wendy's Twitter tactic. Buzz does not sell hamburgers. Oreo's got a lot of buzz when they did that tweet about the Super Bowl blackout. There's no evidence they sold even one more cookie. They're not in the business of entertaining us. So Jaguar isn't going to sell more cars because people like you and I are talking about their re-logoing. What's going to make them sell cars is customer traction. What they need to do is find 50 people who have authority and get them in a car that changes them somehow, that transforms them. (40:26): And it's interesting if you think about two things that Tesla did right at the beginning with the model S. The first one is, according to someone I know who worked there at the time, the number one thing people would talk about when they saw you in the parking lot of the supermarket was the door handles, because the door handles popped out. They popped out in a way that's annoying and dangerous, but it was noticeable. So there was a conversation. (40:52): And then what would happen is they'd say, what do you think of it? And you'd say, get in the car and you'd switch to ludicrous mode and you'd drive at zero to 60 in 2.4 seconds and they'd start screaming. This was fun for you and told a story to the passenger. This is how customer traction begins because I can't do that in a different car, right? Compare this to the clown car, the Cybertruck, which was intentionally divisive and most people don't want to not only drive one but have one on their block because divisiveness is not selling. That what's selling is being of utility, to help someone get what they want. So here you have a category, the pickup truck, the number one category for all cars in the United States, just sitting there waiting to be taken. You can cross the chasm if you're someone like Tesla. And instead, they decide to pull a stunt, and that's not okay. It's not good product management. It's not good marketing.
turns.zh: 你或许还记得国际煎饼屋（International House of Pancakes）曾虚假宣称更名为国际汉堡屋（International House of Burgers）并设计新标志，只为博眼球。这不过是温蒂汉堡（Wendy's）的营销手段。引发话题并不能促进汉堡销量。奥利奥（Oreo）在超级碗停电事件后发推引发热议，却未见销量提升。他们根本不是娱乐公众的企业。所以捷豹不会因为你我谈论其新标志而销量提升。真正能推动销量的关键在于客户口碑。他们需要找到50位有影响力的人，带他们体验能改变他们认知的车型。（40:26）：有趣的是，想想特斯拉（Tesla）Model S刚推出时做对的两件事。据我认识的一位当时在特斯拉工作的人透露，人们在超市停车场看到Model S时，最常谈论的就是车门把手，因为把手会弹出。这种设计既烦人又危险，但确实引人注目。于是便有了话题。（40:52）：接下来，他们会问：“你觉得怎么样？”你回答：“上车试试吧。”然后切换到“荒唐模式”，2.4秒内从0加速到60英里/小时，乘客们尖叫连连。这既娱乐了乘客，又向对方传递了一个故事。这才是客户口碑的起点——毕竟我可没法在其他车上体验到这种乐趣，对吧？再看看特斯拉的另一个车型——Cybertruck。这款故意引发分裂的车型，大多数人既不想驾驶它，也不想让它停在自家街区，因为分裂性并不能促进销售。真正能卖得出去的，必须实用，帮助人们达成目标。现在你手握一个品类——皮卡车，这个美国最畅销的品类，正静静等待被开发。如果你像特斯拉一样有远见，完全可以跨越鸿沟。然而他们却选择玩花招，这实在不可取。这既不是优秀的产品管理，也不是明智的营销策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. So you think Cybertruck are not going to be a success?
turns.zh: 有意思。所以你认为Cybertruck不会成功？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: Well, I think, compared to what, right? So the Ford F-150 some years has made more than a hundred percent of Ford's profit, meaning without the Ford 150 pickup truck, there is no Ford. That's how big a category that is. You have a car with momentum and a public company where you've earned the trust of a lot of people. Now you have a category, pickup trucks, that are purchased for a very specific reason to show your neighbors you care about utility. Even if you never use the bed, that's the story of driving a pickup truck. So now, if you bring people in that category who are inherently skeptical of change and inherently skeptical of design trickery, something that is nothing but change and design trickery, no, they're not going to adopt it. You could have sold an enormous number of people who might've bought a Ford 150 instead. That crossing of the chasm is how you become really significant.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得得和什么相比才行，对吧？所以福特F-150皮卡多年来为福特公司贡献了超过100%的利润，意思就是没有F-150皮卡，就没有福特这个品牌。这足以说明这个品类的重要性。你手握一款势头正盛的车型，又是一家赢得了众多公众信任的上市公司。现在你又要面对一个品类——皮卡车，而购买皮卡的人往往有特定需求，就是要向邻居展示自己对实用性的重视。即便你从不使用皮卡后厢，这也是驾驶皮卡的意义所在。所以当你面对一群对变革和设计噱头天生持怀疑态度的群体时，他们绝不会轻易接受这些创新。原本本可以卖给大量福特150皮卡潜在客户的车型，就这样白白流失了。而跨越这道鸿沟，才能真正成就非凡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like this alone could be its own separate podcast conversation. I wish we had more time. I'm going to ask one last question, and this is a quote that I found of yours that I also love that is reminiscent of Elon Musk, actually, as we were just talking about this. "The secret to leadership is simple. Do what you believe. Paint a picture of the future. Go there. People will follow." Can you just talk about that?
turns.zh: 我觉得光是这段内容就能单独开一期播客讨论了。真希望我们有更多时间。最后我想问一个问题，我之前发现你说过一句很棒的话，让人联想到埃隆·马斯克。我们刚刚还聊到这句话：“领导力的秘诀很简单。做你所信仰的。描绘未来的图景。然后去实现它。人们会追随你的。” 能否请你谈谈这个观点？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: I might be a little too glib because what I need to highlight is the painting the picture of the future needs to be based in empathy. You can't paint a picture of where you want to go. You have to paint a picture of where they want to go, and it's this non-narcissism that is where professionals do their work. That you are not entitled to raise money, you're not entitled to have market share, you're not entitled to get a good price because you worked hard. What we can do is be of service. We can open the door to help people get to where they always wanted to go. It's very difficult to change what people want, but it's pretty helpful to offer people a chance to get to where they always wanted to go in the first place.
turns.zh: 我可能说得太轻率了，因为我要强调的是，描绘未来图景必须基于同理心。你不能只描绘自己想去的地方，而要描绘人们想去的地方。这种非自恋的思维，才是专业人士开展工作的关键所在。你无权筹集资金，无权占据市场份额，也无权因为努力工作就获得高价。能为人们服务才是正道。我们要为人们打开通往理想之地的门户。改变人们的需求很难，但为人们提供通往理想之地的机会，却相当有益。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Seth, this was a dream come true. I appreciate you coming on the podcast. I appreciate you saying that. Where can people check out your book? Where should people go to learn more about what you're up to? Anything you want to share.
turns.zh: 塞斯，这次合作真是圆梦了。感谢你做客播客，也感谢你刚才的分享。读者在哪里可以了解你的书？想了解你最新动态的读者该去哪里？你有什么想分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: So I'm not active on social media, but I do have a blog at Seths.blog. If you go to Seths.blog/TIS, you'll find everything you need to know about the book and the strategy deck and the collectible chocolate bar and whatever other thing I've dreamed up in the meantime.
turns.zh: 我不怎么活跃在社交媒体上，但我在Seths.blog上有个博客。如果你访问Seths.blog/TIS，就能找到关于书籍、策略卡片、收藏巧克力棒以及我近期构想的其他项目的所有信息。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Chocolate. Seth, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 巧克力。塞斯，非常感谢你今天的到来。

turns.speaker: Seth Godin
turns.en: These were great questions, Lenny, I could talk to you all day. Thank you,
turns.zh: 莱尼，这些问题太棒了，我能和你聊一整天。谢谢你，

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I appreciate that. Same. Bye everyone. (44:52): Thank you so much for listening. turns.zh: 我也很感激。再见大家。（44:52）：非常感谢收听。如果你觉得这期节目有价值，可以在Apple Podcasts、Spotify或你喜欢的播客应用上订阅。也请考虑给我们评分或留下评论，这对其他听众找到播客非常有帮助。你可以在LennysPodcast.com上找到所有往期节目或了解更多信息。下一期节目见。
